But this table has no pattern at all.
That is fine, because the real question is simpler than a pattern.
A function gives exactly one output for each input.
If one input ever gets two different outputs, it is not a function.
Let's walk the inputs one at a time.
Input 1 gives 3. Input 2 gives 5.
Keep going and every input shows up exactly once, with one output each.
So this table is a function.
Now watch this one.
Input 2 shows up twice. Once it gives 6, and once it gives 8.
That is button A handing you chips one day and a cookie the next. Not a function.
Here is one that looks suspicious. Every single input gives 5.
But two buttons are allowed to give you the same snack.
Each input still has just one output, so this is a function.
Don't say "not a function" just because an output repeats.
Only a repeated input with two different outputs breaks the rule.
Seeing 4 go in does not tell you what comes out. There is no guessing here.
You have to follow the rule, and follow it in the right order.
Put the input into the rule in place of x.
Then work it out, multiplying first, to get the output.
Our input is 4.
So everywhere the rule says input, we write a 4 instead.
That gives us 3 × 4 − 2.
Multiply before you subtract.
So an input of 4 gives an output of 10.

Mathematicians write this same rule a shorter way.
It looks like f(x) = 3x − 2, and the x is just the input.
So f(4) means the output when the input is 4, which we already found: 10.

Don't subtract before you multiply.

Plant A gets taller every week, and so does Plant B.

When x goes up in equal steps, check how much y changes each step.
The same change every time makes a straight line.
Start with Plant A. Each week x goes up 1.
The height goes 1, 3, 5, 7, so that is up 2, up 2, up 2, the same step every single time.
Plot those points and they sit on one straight line.
Now Plant B. It goes 0, 1, 4, 9.
That is up 1, then up 3, then up 5.
The steps keep getting bigger, so the points bend upward instead of staying in line.
Plant A changed by the same amount every step, so its points make a straight line.
We have a name for a table like that.

If x jumps 1 and then jumps 2, y should jump twice as far the second time, and it is still linear.

The amount that repeats each time goes in front of x.
The amount paid once is added on.
Start with the $25. You pay that one time, right at the start.
So at 0 months, before a single month has gone by, you have already paid $25.
Now the part that repeats. Each month adds another $10, so x months add 10 × x.
We write that as 10x.
Check it at 3 months: 25 + 10 × 3 = 55.
Put the two pieces together. The cost is 10 times the months, plus 25.
Use y for the cost and x for the months and you get y = 10x + 25.
Now those 24 months take one line.

Don't put the one-time amount in front of x.

Read the graph from left to right.
Up means the amount is growing, down means it is shrinking, and flat means it is not changing.
Start at the left. From hour 0 to hour 2 the graph climbs.
The distance from home is growing, so Sam is riding away from home.
Now the next piece. From hour 2 to hour 4 the graph runs flat at 6 miles.
The distance is not changing at all.
Sam has stopped for a rest.
Two of these pieces go up, but not in the same way.
From hour 4 to hour 6 the graph climbs only 2 miles, and from hour 0 to hour 2 it climbed 6.
Steeper means faster.
And from hour 6 to hour 10 it heads back down, because Sam is riding home.
Here is the big one.
Don't read the graph as a picture of a hill.
Going down does not mean Sam is riding downhill. It means he is getting closer to home.

You need the new spot of every single corner.
In a slide, every point moves the same distance in the same direction.
Change every x by the same amount, and every y by the same amount.

Move it 4 to the right, and the x goes from 1 up to 5.
Move it 2 up, and the y goes from 1 to 3.

Right adds to x, and left takes it away.
Up adds to y, and down takes it away.
For our slide of 4 right and 2 up, every point (x, y) becomes (x + 4, y + 2).
Don't mix up which number is which.
Right and left change x, and x is the first number. Up and down change y, the second one.

Watch what happens: it comes out the same way up.

Look down the list. Every x stayed exactly where it was, and every y flipped its sign.

It swings from the right side across to the left. A at (2, 1) lands on (−2, 1).
This time the y stays put, and it is the x that changes sign.

Follow corner A. It is at (3, 1), which is 3 right and 1 up from the center.
Now turn that arm a quarter turn, the way a clock hand would go backward.
It points 1 left and 3 up instead. So A′ sits at (−1, 3).

The two of them swapped places, and then the new first number changed sign.

So A at (3, 1) goes straight to (−3, −1).

In a box you could stack little cubes and just count them up.
A can is round, though.
Line cubes up against that curved side and you get gaps everywhere.
A cylinder is a stack of circles.
Find the area of the circle, 3.14 × radius × radius, then multiply by the height.
Start at the circle on the bottom.
From the center out to the edge is 2 in, so that is the radius.
The area of a circle is 3.14 times the radius times the radius.
That gives us 12.56 square inches in one layer.
Now stack that circle up the can.
Every inch of height is one more layer of 12.56.
The can is 5 in tall, so we get 5 layers.
One layer is 12.56, and we want 5 of them.
Written out in one go, that is 3.14 × 2 × 2 × 5, the circle and then the height.
So your can holds 62.8 cubic inches of soup.
Don't use the distance all the way across.
This can is 4 in across, but the rule wants the radius, and that is 2 in.
Watch what happens as you go up this cup.
A cone is not the same all the way up.
Its circles get smaller and smaller until they shrink to a point, so there is no one circle to stack again and again.
A cone holds 1/3 of the cylinder with the same bottom and height.
Find the cylinder, then divide by 3.
Try this one for real.
Fill the cone with water, then pour it into a cylinder with the same bottom and the same height.
One pour, and the cylinder is only a third full.
It takes 3 whole cones to fill it.
So forget the cone for a moment.
Build the cylinder with that same bottom and that same height.
Circle times height: 3.14 × 3 × 3 × 4 = 113.04 cubic centimeters.
Now bring the cone back.
It holds one third of what that cylinder holds.
Your paper cup holds 37.68 cubic centimeters of water.
Here is where people lose the point.
Don't stop once you have the cylinder.
A cone holds only one third of it, so you have to divide by 3 at the end.
Here is the problem with a ball.
It has no flat bottom to stack layers on, and no straight height to stack them up.
Our cylinder rule has nothing to hold on to.
A ball fills 2/3 of the can that fits around it.
